# ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression

###### Abstract

Large reasoning models (LRMs) achieve strong performance via extended
chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, yet suffer from excessive token
consumption and high inference latency. Existing reinforcement learning
(RL) approaches for CoT compression rely on uniform, static length
penalties that neglect model capability dynamics and problem-level
difficulty variation. We propose ExpThink, an RL framework that
addresses both dimensions through two complementary mechanisms. First,
_experience-guided reward shaping_ tracks the shortest correct solution
found so far for each problem and applies a three-tier reward: full
credit for concise correct responses, discounted credit for verbose
correct ones, and zero for incorrect ones. The threshold tightens
automatically with model improvement, forming a self-evolving curriculum
that requires no manual scheduling. Second, _difficulty-adaptive
advantage_ replaces standard deviation normalization with correct-count
normalization, yielding monotonically difficulty-scaled gradients that
amplify learning on hard problems to preserve accuracy while suppressing
gradients on easy ones to encourage brevity. Together, these mechanisms
enforce an accuracy-first, compression-second training objective.
Experiments on multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate
that ExpThink reduces average response length by up to 77% while
simultaneously improving accuracy, achieving up to $`3\times`$ higher
accuracy-efficiency ratio (accuracy divided by average token count) than
the vanilla baseline and outperforming existing RL-based compression
methods on both metrics.

## 1 Introduction

Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) such as OpenAI-o1, DeepSeek-R1, and
Qwen3 \[[36](#bib.bib1), [7](#bib.bib2), [40](#bib.bib9)\] have shown
that extended Chain-of-Thought (CoT) sequences substantially improve
complex reasoning \[[43](#bib.bib3)\]. However, these models produce
lengthy reasoning traces regardless of problem difficulty, incurring
redundant computation, high latency, and verbose
outputs \[[9](#bib.bib4), [10](#bib.bib30), [11](#bib.bib31)\]. We
quantify this inefficiency via _intelligence per token_ (IPT), defined
as the ratio of correctness to generation length, and find that current
LRMs achieve strong accuracy at the cost of poor IPT.

Inference-time strategies such as adaptive routing and early exits
reduce output length but leave the model’s inherent verbosity
unchanged \[[49](#bib.bib10), [18](#bib.bib5), [51](#bib.bib11)\].
Supervised fine-tuning on distilled concise traces is prone to
distribution shift and depends heavily on demonstration
quality \[[44](#bib.bib6), [52](#bib.bib7)\]. Reinforcement learning
(RL) offers a more principled path by jointly rewarding correctness and
brevity, and methods such as L1, ThinkPrune, LC-R1, and Laser have
demonstrated substantial token reduction with minimal accuracy
loss \[[1](#bib.bib12), [8](#bib.bib13), [17](#bib.bib16),
[28](#bib.bib14)\]. Yet all existing RL approaches share a structural
limitation
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression")):
each epoch is treated as an independent episode, discarding all
trajectory information after every update.

![Refer to caption](2605.07501v2/method_overview10.png)

Figure 1: Top: Standard RL treats each epoch independently, discarding
all trajectory information after each update. Bottom: ExpThink
accumulates successful trajectories into an experience buffer, enabling
a self-evolving compression curriculum that tightens automatically as
the policy improves.

This epoch-independent design neglects a basic fact: the policy’s
capability is not stationary. As training progresses, problems that once
required lengthy derivations become solvable in fewer steps, yet fixed
length penalties assume a static compression goal throughout. The
training process itself already produces exactly the signal needed: each
time the model finds a short correct solution, it establishes a tighter
per-problem compression bound, tracing a natural coarse-to-fine
curriculum. Standard RL discards this signal after every update, never
using it to recalibrate the reward.

We propose ExpThink to exploit this signal. The framework maintains an
_experience buffer_ that records the shortest correct solution per
problem across all past epochs, defining an adaptive reward threshold
that tightens automatically as the policy improves, without any manual
scheduling. Our key contributions are:

- •
  We identify a structural limitation shared by existing RL-based CoT
  compression methods: historical trajectory information accumulated
  during training is discarded after each update and never used to
  recalibrate the compression objective as the policy improves.
- •
  We propose ExpThink, an experience-driven RL framework with a
  self-evolving compression curriculum, an experience-guided three-tier
  reward, and difficulty-adaptive advantage estimation that jointly
  optimize accuracy and brevity.
- •
  ExpThink reduces average response length by up to 77% while
  consistently improving accuracy across all model scales, with stable
  training dynamics, achieving up to $`3\times`$ higher IPT than the
  vanilla baseline and outperforming all prior RL-based compression
  methods on both metrics.

## 2 Preliminary Observation

We begin with an empirical observation that motivates our approach.
Using the setup described in
Section [4](#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression"),
we train a reasoning model on DeepScaleR for approximately 55 steps and
track two per-prompt statistics: the _batch mean length_ $`\bar{\ell}`$,
the mean response length over all prompts at the current step, and the
_mean shortest correct (historical)_ $`\ell^{*}`$, the running minimum
of correct response length across all past training steps averaged over
prompts.

Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2 Preliminary Observation ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression")
reveals a striking divergence between these two curves over the first
$`{\sim}`$55 training steps. The blue curve (batch mean length) starts
at approximately 8,000 tokens and decreases only modestly to around
6,300 tokens by the end of training.

Figure 2: Response length dynamics during RL training on DeepScaleR.

In contrast, the red curve (mean shortest correct, historical) begins at
approximately 5,500 tokens and drops sharply to around 1,000 tokens,
demonstrating that the model rapidly learns to solve problems far more
concisely.

By step 55, the gap between the two curves widens to $`\Delta`$5,400
tokens: the model _can_ produce short correct solutions, yet its average
rollout length remains far above this self-demonstrated lower bound.
This exposes a structural inefficiency: the short correct trajectories
already produced during training are discarded after each update and
never used to recalibrate the length signal. This observation motivates
a simple principle: _reuse the shortest correct trajectories from past
rollouts as an adaptive, per-problem compression target_. We formalize
this idea in the next section.

## 3 ExpThink

The key insight driving ExpThink is that standard RL training discards
two valuable signals after every update: evidence that certain problems
_can_ be solved correctly, which establishes a per-problem achievability
bound on response length, and evidence that the LRM _already solves_
many problems consistently, which identifies where gradient budget is
wasted on correctness and should shift to brevity. ExpThink captures
both signals through a minimal modification to
DAPO \[[48](#bib.bib27)\]: a running experience buffer that converts the
first signal into an adaptive reward threshold, and a count-based
advantage normalizer that converts the second into difficulty-weighted
gradients.

Throughout this section we assume a training distribution
$`\mathcal{D}`$ of queries $`q`$ with ground-truth answers $`y^{\ast}`$.
For each $`q`$, the old policy samples a group of $`G`$ rollouts
$`\{o_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}`$, where $`o_{i}`$ has token length $`|o_{i}|`$
and produces a final answer $`y_{i}`$. We write
$`|\mathcal{C}_{q}|=\sum_{i=1}^{G}\mathbb{I}[y_{i}=y^{\ast}]`$ for the
number of correct rollouts in the group.

### 3.1 Experience-Guided Reward Shaping

A binary correctness reward treats every correct rollout identically and
therefore gives the policy no reason to prefer shorter derivations over
longer ones. Length penalties can address this, but the penalty is
typically static: it is fixed ahead of time and remains unchanged as the
LRM improves, even though the same problem might admit progressively
shorter solutions over the course of training. We observe that every
correct rollout the LRM produces is already direct evidence of an
achievable length bound on that problem, and that these bounds
monotonically tighten as the policy improves. ExpThink uses these
running bounds as the reward signal.

Concretely, we maintain a global dictionary $`\mathcal{E}`$ that stores,
for every training prompt $`q`$, the shortest correct trajectory length
ever observed. Writing $`\ell^{*,(t)}_{q}`$ for this value at step
$`t`$, the update after each batch is

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\ell^{*,(t)}_{q}\;=\;\min\!\left(\,\ell^{*,(t-1)}_{q},\;\;\min_{\,i\,:\,y_{i}=y^{\ast}\,}\,|o_{i}|\,\right),
``` |  | (1) |

where the inner minimum is $`+\infty`$ whenever no rollout in the
current group is correct, leaving the buffer unchanged. Prompts that
have never yielded a correct trajectory are initialized with
$`\ell^{*,(0)}_{q}=L_{\max}`$, the training context budget. Because
([1](#S3.E1 "In 3.1 Experience-Guided Reward Shaping ‣ 3 ExpThink ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression"))
takes a running minimum, $`\ell^{*}_{q}`$ is non-increasing throughout
training and traces an implicit, per-prompt curriculum whose target
tightens exactly as the LRM discovers shorter solutions, without any
manually scheduled annealing.

The buffer defines a per-problem achievability bound, but a binary
correct/incorrect reward cannot exploit it: declaring a verbose-correct
response “wrong” would strip the policy of its only positive signal on
hard problems where short solutions have not yet been discovered.
Instead, we define a three-tier reward that preserves positive signal
for every correct response while imposing graded compression pressure:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r_{i}^{\text{exp}}\;=\;\begin{cases}1,&y_{i}=y^{\ast}\;\text{and}\;|o_{i}|\leq\ell^{*}_{q}(1+\alpha),\\[2.0pt]
r_{\text{pen}},&y_{i}=y^{\ast}\;\text{and}\;|o_{i}|>\ell^{*}_{q}(1+\alpha),\\[2.0pt]
0,&y_{i}\neq y^{\ast}.\end{cases}
``` |  | (2) |

The tolerance $`\alpha\in[0,+\infty)`$ provides a soft margin around the
historical minimum, and $`r_{\text{pen}}\in[0,1)`$ assigns correct but
verbose rollouts a discounted reward. The discount distinguishes concise
solutions from verbose ones without outright punishing correctness, so
the policy still receives positive signal whenever it gets the answer
right.

![Refer to caption](2605.07501v2/pipeline3.png)

Figure 3: Overview of the ExpThink framework. For each query, the policy
samples a group of rollouts, from which an experience buffer extracts
the shortest correct trajectory seen so far; this running minimum is
used to shape a pass-rate gated, three-tier reward, which is in turn
combined with a count-based advantage estimator to produce
difficulty-adaptive gradients.

### 3.2 Difficulty-Adaptive Advantage

Prior work has proposed reshaping the reward to reflect problem
difficulty \[[28](#bib.bib14), [27](#bib.bib35)\], yet intervening at
the reward level is insufficient: the per-group standard deviation
$`\sigma`$ used in GRPO is a concave function of $`|\mathcal{C}_{q}|`$,
peaking when half the rollouts are correct and vanishing at both
extremes. A prompt the policy almost never solves and one it almost
always solves therefore receive nearly identical normalization, and
whatever difficulty signal was injected at the reward level is silently
cancelled before reaching the gradient. We resolve this by replacing
$`\sigma`$ with $`|\mathcal{C}_{q}|`$ directly:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{A}_{i}\;=\;\frac{r_{i}-\mu}{|\mathcal{C}_{q}|+\epsilon},\qquad\mu\;=\;\frac{1}{G}\sum_{j=1}^{G}r_{j},
``` |  | (3) |

where $`\epsilon>0`$ and the denominator is clamped to $`1`$ when
$`|\mathcal{C}_{q}|=0`$. Because $`|\mathcal{C}_{q}|`$ counts exactly
how many rollouts the policy solved correctly, gradient magnitude is now
strictly decreasing in $`|\mathcal{C}_{q}|`$, preserving difficulty
awareness all the way to the parameter update. This substitution also
reveals a clean structural property: the advantage gap between a
short-correct and a long-correct rollout in the same group equals
$`(1-r_{\mathrm{pen}})/(|\mathcal{C}_{q}|+\epsilon)`$, which is the
selective pressure the gradient exerts on length. On hard prompts this
gap is a minor fraction of a large overall advantage, so the update
drives correctness; on easy prompts the overall advantage shrinks and
this gap becomes the dominant signal, so the update drives brevity. We
term this the *accuracy-first, compression-second* learning dynamic: the
LRM is pushed toward conciseness only where correctness is already
reliable, with no manual scheduling required. In combination with the
self-evolving threshold from
Eq. ([1](#S3.E1 "In 3.1 Experience-Guided Reward Shaping ‣ 3 ExpThink ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression")),
the two mechanisms jointly induce an implicit curriculum along both the
accuracy and length axes.

Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.1 Experience-Guided Reward Shaping ‣ 3 ExpThink ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression")
illustrates the complete per-step data flow, highlighting how the
experience buffer and the advantage normalizer interact within the DAPO
training loop.

### 3.3 Training Objective

The shaped reward $`r_{i}`$ and the reweighted advantage $`\hat{A}_{i}`$
replace their counterparts in the standard DAPO \[[48](#bib.bib27)\]
objective. Broadcasting $`\hat{A}_{i}`$ across all tokens of $`o_{i}`$
to obtain $`\hat{A}_{i,t}`$, and writing
$`\rho_{i,t}(\theta)=\pi_{\theta}(o_{i,t}\mid q,o_{i,<t})/\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(o_{i,t}\mid q,o_{i,<t})`$
for the token-level importance ratio, ExpThink optimizes

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{J}(\theta)\;=`$ | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{(q,\,y^{\ast})\sim\mathcal{D},\,\{o_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(\cdot\mid q)}`$ |  | (4) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\left[\,\frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^{G}|o_{i}|}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\sum_{t=1}^{|o_{i}|}\min\!\left(\rho_{i,t}(\theta)\,\hat{A}_{i,t},\;\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\rho_{i,t}(\theta),\,1-\varepsilon_{\text{low}},\,1+\varepsilon_{\text{high}}\right)\hat{A}_{i,t}\right)\,\right].`$ |  |  |

The asymmetric clipping thresholds
$`\varepsilon_{\text{low}}<\varepsilon_{\text{high}}`$ are inherited
from DAPO and permit larger updates in the favorable direction while
retaining a conservative lower bound on the unfavorable side.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Setup

#### Models.

We evaluate ExpThink on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B,
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen3-8B \[[7](#bib.bib2),
[40](#bib.bib9)\] as backbone models.

#### Training.

Training is conducted on the DeepScaleR dataset \[[31](#bib.bib21)\],
which contains approximately 40K mathematical problems with calibrated
difficulty levels. We set $`\alpha=0.1`$ and $`r_{\text{pen}}=0.5`$ as
default; full hyperparameters are provided in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Training Hyperparameters ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression").

#### Evaluation benchmarks.

We evaluate on five standard mathematical reasoning benchmarks:
AIME24 \[[6](#bib.bib22)\], AMC23 \[[33](#bib.bib23)\],
MATH-500 \[[26](#bib.bib52)\], Minerva Math \[[20](#bib.bib25)\], and
OlympiadBench \[[14](#bib.bib26)\]. To further assess out-of-domain
generalization, we additionally evaluate on
LiveCodeBench \[[19](#bib.bib29)\] for code reasoning,
GPQA-Diamond \[[38](#bib.bib36)\] for graduate-level scientific question
answering, and MMLU \[[15](#bib.bib28)\] for broad multitask language
understanding. Detailed descriptions of all benchmarks are provided in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Datasets ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression").

#### Evaluation protocol.

We report Pass@1 accuracy, average response token length, and
Intelligence per Token (IPT), defined as accuracy divided by response
length in kilotokens. To quantify efficiency gains, we additionally
report $`\Delta`$Acc and $`\Delta`$Token as the average relative change
(%) across all benchmarks with respect to the Vanilla baseline.
Evaluation runs are replicated 16 times on AIME24, 8 times on AMC23, and
once on the remaining benchmarks, which have larger test sets. Context
length and sampling hyperparameters follow
DeepSeek-R1 \[[7](#bib.bib2)\].

#### Baselines.

We compare against five representative RL-based methods spanning
aggressive and conservative length-control strategies:
LC-R1 \[[5](#bib.bib15)\], Laser \[[28](#bib.bib14)\],
AutoThink \[[41](#bib.bib18)\], AdaptThink \[[50](#bib.bib19)\], and
JET \[[12](#bib.bib20)\]. Detailed descriptions of each baseline are
provided in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Detailed Descriptions of Baselines ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression").

### 4.2 Main Results

Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression")
and
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression")
reveal three consistent patterns across all model scales.

(1) Simultaneous accuracy and compression gains. ExpThink is the only
method that simultaneously improves accuracy *and* achieves the shortest
responses across all three backbone sizes, a combination no baseline
achieves on any single model. Token usage falls by 65.5% on the 1.5B
model with an average accuracy gain of $`+`$4.53%, and by 77.2% on
Qwen3-8B with $`+`$5.33%, ruling out scale as an explanation.
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression")
shows that accuracy and brevity improve in two distinct phases rather
than competing with each other. Batch accuracy climbs from 68.0% to
76.5% over 300 training steps while response length drops by 69.4%. The
temporary accuracy dip around steps 100–150 marks the period of fastest
length-target tightening, after which accuracy rebounds at a permanently
lower token count. This phased behaviour is built into the experience
buffer: the length target $`\ell^{*}_{q}`$ is only tightened after the
model has already produced a shorter correct answer, so the model is
never pressured to be brief before it can be correct.

(2) Larger models benefit more. IPT increases steadily with model size:
from 7.23 to 23.29 on the 1.5B model, from 11.15 to 32.84 on 7B, and
from 8.64 to 51.04 on Qwen3-8B. Stronger models find shorter correct
solutions earlier in training, which tightens the experience buffer
sooner and drives further compression. On Qwen3-8B, MATH-500 responses
shrink to just 755.7 tokens at 94.2% accuracy, suggesting the model can
solve most problems with very little text.

(3) Fixed penalties cannot avoid the accuracy–brevity trade-off. Methods
with aggressive length penalties, such as LC-R1, compress responses
substantially but hurt accuracy; conservative methods such as Laser and
JET preserve accuracy but stall near $`{\sim}50\%`$ or less compression.
The underlying reason is the same for both: without any memory of past
training trajectories, the compression target stays fixed even as the
model improves. ExpThink addresses this by recording the shortest
correct solution found so far for each problem and using it as an
adaptive target, reaching 65.5% and 77.2% token reduction on 1.5B and
Qwen3-8B with no accuracy loss. Among 1.5B baselines, AdaptThink is the
closest competitor at $`-`$57.3% tokens, yet its IPT of 18.04 is still
29% below ExpThink, and its Minerva accuracy of 22.1 trails ExpThink’s
29.0, showing that even adaptive thresholds fall short without
trajectory memory.

### 4.3 Ablation Studies

We ablate the penalty coefficient $`r_{\text{pen}}`$ and the advantage
normalization on the 1.5B model
(Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Discounted reward 𝑟_"pen". ‣ 4.3 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression"),
Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Discounted reward 𝑟_"pen". ‣ 4.3 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression")).

#### Discounted reward $`r_{\text{pen}}`$.

With the harshest length penalty ($`r_{\text{pen}}=0.0`$), verbose but
correct answers receive zero reward—identical to wrong answers—so the
model learns to output very short but mostly wrong answers: AIME24
accuracy collapses to 7.92% and MATH-500 to 43.6%, far below the
unmodified baseline. Relaxing the penalty to 0.3 partially restores
accuracy but is still too aggressive to maintain the accuracy-first
training progression needed for stable learning. The default value of
0.5 strikes the best balance, yielding MATH-500 accuracy of 82.2% at
1,417 tokens and AIME24 accuracy of 28.8% at 5,350 tokens with an
average IPT of 23.3, as reflected in the stable training curves in
Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Discounted reward 𝑟_"pen". ‣ 4.3 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression")(a)
and (b). A weaker penalty of $`r_{\text{pen}}=0.7`$ raises accuracy on
most benchmarks by 2–7 percentage points but reduces Minerva accuracy by
2.9 points, increases average response length by over 50%, and cuts IPT
by roughly 37%
(Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Discounted reward 𝑟_"pen". ‣ 4.3 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression")(c)),
making it impractical under standard compute budgets.

Figure 5: Training dynamics under different $`r_{\text{pen}}`$ settings
and advantage functions. (a) AMC23 Pass@1 over training steps.
(b) Average response length (tokens) over training steps. (c) Wall-clock
time per training step.

#### Count-based advantage normalization.

When the correct-count $`|\mathcal{C}_{q}|`$ is replaced by the standard
deviation $`\sigma`$ as the advantage denominator (Std. GRPO adv.),
accuracy stays similar but the model generates 1.6 to 1.8 times more
tokens per response, dropping average IPT from 23.3 to 14.5; response
length never reaches the compact levels seen in ExpThink
(Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Discounted reward 𝑟_"pen". ‣ 4.3 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression")(b)).
The reason is that $`\sigma`$ does not distinguish between easy and hard
problems: it assigns similar gradient magnitudes to both, so the model
receives no signal to be brief on easy questions and no extra push to be
correct on hard ones, breaking the accuracy-first pattern that ExpThink
relies on.

### 4.4 Dissecting Compressed Reasoning Traces

#### Overthinking keyword suppression.

(a)

(b)

Figure 6: Analysis of ExpThink’s behaviour. (a) Overthinking suppression
across keywords and datasets; (b) Difficulty-adaptive behaviour on
MATH-500.

We segment reasoning traces at double-newline boundaries and count
overthinking indicators following [Lu et al. \[30\]](#bib.bib8): {But,
Wait, Alternatively, However, Hmm, Not sure, Going back, Backtrack,
Another}, which are lexical markers of hesitation, self-correction, or
exploratory branching. As shown in
Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Overthinking keyword suppression. ‣ 4.4 Dissecting Compressed Reasoning Traces ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression")(a-left),
ExpThink reduces the total frequency of these keywords by 78.8%, with
But and Wait, the two most common ones, falling by 79% and 86%
respectively, while accuracy improves from 50.3% to 52.3%. The number of
reasoning steps also drops by 63.1%, from 218.3 to 80.6 steps on average
(Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Overthinking keyword suppression. ‣ 4.4 Dissecting Compressed Reasoning Traces ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression")(a-right)).
The reduction is steeper on Minerva than on AIME, where problems
genuinely require longer derivations. This pattern shows that ExpThink
primarily cuts unnecessary hedging and backtracking, rather than
shortening all responses uniformly.

#### Difficulty-adaptive compression.

Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Overthinking keyword suppression. ‣ 4.4 Dissecting Compressed Reasoning Traces ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression")(b)
reports accuracy and response length across the five difficulty tiers of
MATH-500. As expected, easier problems are compressed more aggressively:
Level-1 responses shrink by 79.8% while Level-5 shrinks by 65.4%. This
happens because easy problems are solved correctly by more rollouts,
giving them a larger $`|\mathcal{C}_{q}|`$ that weakens the advantage
signal and pushes the model toward brevity. For harder problems where
fewer rollouts succeed, the stronger advantage signal prioritises
getting the answer right over being short, which is why accuracy gains
are larger at higher difficulty: Level-4 improves by 6.3 percentage
points and Level-3 by 2.9 percentage points. Even so, compression
remains substantial at the top tier: Level-5 saves approximately 4,740
tokens per response on average, compared with roughly 1,767 at Level-1.

### 4.5 Trajectory Diversity and Inference-Time Scaling

(a) Trajectory diversity across methods

(b) Majority@$`k`$ scaling under token budget

Figure 7: Inference-time analysis on AIME24. (a) Average response length
vs. per-problem coefficient of variation (CV) of response length.
(b) Majority@$`k`$ accuracy versus total inference tokens
consumed.DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, 512 samples per problem.

Shorter traces allow more parallel rollouts within a fixed compute
budget. We sample $`k\in\{1,2,4,\ldots,512\}`$ independent responses per
problem on AIME24 and report majority-voting accuracy against total
tokens consumed.

#### Diversity of reasoning trajectories.

To understand *why* ExpThink scales better with repeated sampling, we
measure the per-problem coefficient of variation (CV) of response length
across 512 rollouts, which captures how much a model’s solution length
varies from one attempt to the next. As shown in
Figure [7](#S4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 4.5 Trajectory Diversity and Inference-Time Scaling ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression")(a),
ExpThink has the highest CV at 0.664 with an average response length of
only 5.5K tokens, while the Vanilla baseline produces consistently long
outputs averaging 12.3K tokens and a much lower CV of 0.291. In other
words, ExpThink sometimes finds a short solution and sometimes takes
longer, exploring varied reasoning paths rather than always producing
responses of similar length.

#### Majority-voting scaling.

This diversity translates directly into better performance under a fixed
token budget. As shown in
Figure [7](#S4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 4.5 Trajectory Diversity and Inference-Time Scaling ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression")(b),
the Vanilla baseline stops improving at around 33.3% accuracy from
$`k=16`$ onward, even when up to 6.3 million tokens are spent on
additional samples. ExpThink keeps improving with more samples, reaching
50.0% at $`k=512`$. Given the same budget of 200K tokens, ExpThink
outperforms Vanilla by 12.2 percentage points; put differently, it
reaches Vanilla’s peak accuracy with 289 times fewer tokens. Since
ExpThink’s shorter responses allow more independent attempts within any
fixed budget, and each attempt explores a different reasoning path,
additional samples continue to add value rather than repeating the same
answer.

Table 3: Out-of-domain generalization results. Pass@1 accuracy, average
response length (Token), and Intelligence per Token (IPT) on non-math
benchmarks. $`\Delta`$Acc and $`\Delta`$Token denote the average
relative change with respect to the Vanilla baseline.

Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.6 Generalization to out-of-distribution benchmarks. ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression")
complements the in-domain results in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression")
by testing whether the efficiency gains on math transfer to other task
types without any further fine-tuning. On the 1.5B model, ExpThink
achieves the largest accuracy improvement and the greatest token
reduction among all methods, with an IPT of 27.26 compared with 9.01 for
the Vanilla baseline. The gains are most pronounced on GPQA-Diamond,
where accuracy rises from 16.0 to 25.4, and on MMLU, where it rises from
38.8 to 44.2; these are exactly the types of knowledge-intensive tasks
where models tend to over-deliberate, so the conciseness training is
especially effective. On the 7B model, ExpThink reaches an IPT of 55.39,
nearly 2.7 times the Vanilla baseline’s 20.78, and achieves the best
GPQA-Diamond accuracy of 47.2 among all methods. Overall, these results
show that the compression behaviour learned on math problems carries
over to code and science tasks, reflecting a general reduction in
unnecessary reasoning steps rather than a math-specific shortcut.

## 5 Conclusion

We introduced ExpThink, a reinforcement learning framework that breaks
the epoch-independence assumption of prior CoT compression methods. By
maintaining a per-problem experience buffer of the shortest correct
solution observed across training, ExpThink defines an adaptive reward
threshold that tightens automatically as the policy improves,
eliminating manual schedule design. Paired with count-based advantage
normalization, this self-evolving curriculum allocates optimization
pressure toward correctness on hard problems and toward brevity once
correctness is reliable. Across three backbones, ExpThink consistently
improves the accuracy–efficiency tradeoff, reducing token usage by up to
77% while simultaneously gaining accuracy, and the gains generalize to
out-of-distribution benchmarks including GPQA-Diamond and LiveCodeBench.
These results establish cross-epoch trajectory reuse as a lightweight
and effective principle for training reasoning models with higher
intelligence per token.

#### Limitations.

The training data and primary evaluation are limited to mathematical
reasoning with verifiable answers, and transfer to interactive tool use
or multimodal settings remains to be confirmed. The reward also depends
on reliable answer verification, which may not hold for tasks with
ambiguous or partially correct outputs. A controlled comparison against
DAPO under matched compute, which would further disentangle the
contributions of the experience buffer from those of DAPO-style
training, is also left to future work. Finally, the tolerance margin
$`\alpha`$ and discounted reward $`r_{\text{pen}}`$ that guard against
over-compression are empirical choices; although $`r_{\text{pen}}`$ is
ablated in
Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression"),
a systematic study of $`\alpha`$ sensitivity across diverse domains is
left to future work.

#### Future work.

We plan to extend ExpThink to multimodal reasoning, where concise traces
must preserve visual grounding. A further direction is to store full
trajectories in the experience buffer and perform off-policy replay,
enabling the curriculum to leverage not only length statistics but also
the content of past successful solutions for richer reward shaping and
diversity-aware exploration.

## Appendix A Related Work

### A.1 Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards

A growing body of work leverages historical rollout experience to
improve GRPO training. On the experience-reuse side,
LANPO \[[21](#bib.bib37)\] accumulates past rollouts into a dynamic pool
for cross-sample abstraction, BAPO \[[42](#bib.bib38)\] replays
difficulty-aware batches of previously failed problems,
RPO \[[47](#bib.bib39)\] caches and reuses trajectory prefixes to cut
rollout cost by up to 95%, and SOUP \[[46](#bib.bib40)\] splices
off-policy prefixes with on-policy continuations via importance
weighting. On the reward-shaping side, WS-GRPO\[[34](#bib.bib42)\]
learns prefix-level continue/stop signals from outcome-only data,
F-GRPO \[[37](#bib.bib43)\] applies focal-loss-inspired re-weighting to
shift gradient mass toward rare-correct trajectories,
XRPO \[[2](#bib.bib45)\] sharpens advantages via novelty-aware rollout
allocation, HiLL \[[45](#bib.bib44)\] co-trains a hinter policy to
recover learning signals on hard problems, and STEP \[[4](#bib.bib46)\]
drives adaptive resampling from historical success rates.

### A.2 Reinforcement Learning Based Efficient Reasoning

Reinforcement learning offers a more direct route by jointly rewarding
correctness and brevity, allowing the model to discover shorter valid
paths without annotated demonstrations. The dominant paradigm augments
the reward with a length penalty, as in L1 \[[1](#bib.bib12)\],
ConciseRL \[[8](#bib.bib13)\], ThinkPrune \[[17](#bib.bib16)\], and
LC-R1 \[[5](#bib.bib15)\]. DLER \[[27](#bib.bib35)\] identifies that
naive length penalties can suppress high-entropy exploration tokens
critical for reasoning, proposing a recipe that recovers accuracy while
reducing response length by over 70%. LEASH \[[24](#bib.bib32)\]
introduces an adaptive Lagrangian penalty that dynamically adjusts the
constraint coefficient to accelerate convergence toward a target length.
GR3 \[[25](#bib.bib41)\] replaces additive length penalties with
multiplicative group-relative reward rescaling, eliminating compensatory
optimization shortcuts that arise in standard formulations. Dr.
GRPO \[[29](#bib.bib33)\] corrects an optimization bias in GRPO that
artificially inflates response length for incorrect outputs. Adaptive
frameworks such as DAST and AutoThink \[[39](#bib.bib17),
[41](#bib.bib18), [50](#bib.bib19)\] allocate inference budgets as a
function of estimated problem difficulty, and Laser \[[28](#bib.bib14)\]
combines difficulty-aware penalties with explicit exploration of
incorrect trajectories. ProRL v2 \[[35](#bib.bib34)\] demonstrates that
scheduled cosine length penalties within prolonged RL training enable
sustained improvement over thousands of steps without the model
collapsing to short contexts. Beyond scalar penalties, finer-grained
formulations have emerged: SWAP \[[23](#bib.bib48)\] applies step-level
penalties weighted by each step’s contribution to the correct answer;
FGO \[[13](#bib.bib49)\] subdivides GRPO response groups by length and
entropy to prevent representation collapse during compression;
SCMA \[[3](#bib.bib47)\] uses a dual-agent RL loop that segments
reasoning into chunks and scores each for redundancy;
CEEH \[[32](#bib.bib50)\] selectively regularizes entropy based on
estimated problem difficulty; and [Li et al. \[22\]](#bib.bib51) tie
length penalties to whether the model has already demonstrated ability
to solve a given problem with a shorter response, enabling cross-domain
generalization. Despite their diversity, all these RL methods treat each
training epoch independently: the reward at epoch $`e`$ depends only on
trajectories sampled during epoch $`e`$, leaving cross-epoch compression
progress unused.

## Appendix B Training Hyperparameters

We train all models on 8$`\times`$ A800 80GB GPUs with a global batch
size of 512 and a maximum sequence length of 16,384 tokens. To address
memory constraints under long-context training, we employ Fully Sharded
Data Parallel (FSDP) with CPU offloading.

During optimization, we adopt the GRPO objective with $`\beta=0.001`$
and asymmetric clipping parameters $`\varepsilon_{\text{low}}=0.2`$ and
$`\varepsilon_{\text{high}}=0.28`$. The learning rate is fixed at
$`1\times 10^{-6}`$. We use AdamW as the optimizer with default
parameter settings. For response generation during training, we use
temperature $`=1.0`$ and top-$`p=1.0`$ to encourage exploration; during
validation, we use temperature $`=0.6`$ and top-$`p=0.95`$. Training
runs for 300 update steps. At each step, we sample $`G=16`$ responses
per prompt to construct response groups for GRPO-based advantage
computation. Validation is conducted periodically during training, and
checkpoints are saved every 10 steps for model selection and
reproducibility.

Notably, we do not incorporate KL divergence regularization into the
reward function; the reward signal is computed independently of any KL
penalty term.

## Appendix C Datasets

#### DeepScaleR \[[31](#bib.bib21)\].

DeepScaleR is a curated mathematical reasoning dataset comprising
approximately 40K problems, constructed by scaling up the difficulty
distribution of existing open-source mathematical corpora. It is built
upon a systematic difficulty-aware selection pipeline: problems are
first scored by estimated difficulty, and then progressively sampled to
emphasize challenging instances that demand multi-step derivations,
algebraic manipulation, and advanced problem-solving strategies.
DeepScaleR serves as the training corpus for ExpThink. Its main
strengths lie in its carefully calibrated difficulty gradient, broad
coverage of mathematical topics spanning algebra, geometry, number
theory, and combinatorics.

#### AIME24 \[[6](#bib.bib22)\].

AIME24 consists of the official problems from the 2024 American
Invitational Mathematics Examination (AIME) I and II and has become a
widely used benchmark for evaluating high-level mathematical reasoning.
Its problems typically require sophisticated combinatorial analysis,
geometric constructions, or number-theoretic reasoning, and each admits
a unique three-digit integer answer. In public repositories, AIME24
usually appears as a 30-problem set designed to assess models under
realistic contest conditions.

#### AMC23 \[[33](#bib.bib23)\].

AMC23 is a benchmark derived from the 2023 American Mathematics
Competition, primarily AMC 10 and AMC 12. The problems are reformatted
for model evaluation and usually take the form of multiple-choice or
integer-answer questions, covering core high-school contest topics such
as algebra, geometry, probability, and number theory. The overall
difficulty exceeds routine classroom exercises but remains below that of
AIME and Olympiad-level problems. Compared with AIME24, AMC23 typically
contains a larger number of instances and is therefore commonly used as
a medium-difficulty benchmark.

#### MATH-500 \[[16](#bib.bib24)\].

MATH-500 is a curated subset of 500 competition-level problems drawn
from the MATH dataset. The original MATH dataset contains approximately
12,500 U.S. high-school competition problems, each accompanied by a full
step-by-step solution, and spanning topics such as algebra, geometry,
counting and probability, number theory, and precalculus. Difficulty
levels follow the Art of Problem Solving (AoPS) scale from 1 to 5.
Evaluation is conducted using an exact-match criterion on the final
answer.

#### Minerva Math \[[20](#bib.bib25)\].

Minerva Math is a collection of mathematical and quantitative reasoning
problems assessing formal mathematical and scientific reasoning
capabilities. In publicly released evaluations, roughly 272 problems are
included, primarily sourced from MIT OpenCourseWare and covering
advanced undergraduate- and graduate-level STEM topics such as
solid-state chemistry, astronomy, differential equations, and special
relativity. Compared with pure mathematics competition datasets, Minerva
Math emphasizes cross-disciplinary quantitative problems.

#### OlympiadBench \[[14](#bib.bib26)\].

OlympiadBench is a bilingual multimodal Olympiad-level science benchmark
designed to evaluate the reasoning and problem-solving capabilities of
LLMs using extremely challenging mathematics and physics competition
problems. The dataset aggregates 8,476 questions drawn from
international and national mathematics Olympiads, physics contests, and
the Chinese college entrance examination, spanning both text-only and
image-based multimodal formats. Empirical results indicate that even
state-of-the-art systems achieve relatively low performance,
highlighting the benchmark’s exceptional difficulty.

#### MMLU \[[15](#bib.bib28)\].

MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding) is a comprehensive
benchmark spanning 57 diverse academic subjects, ranging from STEM
disciplines to humanities and social sciences. Each problem is presented
in a four-option multiple-choice format, and the questions are drawn
from real-world examination materials at difficulty levels from
elementary to advanced professional. MMLU is used in our work to assess
out-of-distribution generalization of the efficiency learned by
ExpThink.

#### LiveCodeBench \[[19](#bib.bib29)\].

LiveCodeBench is a holistic and contamination-free benchmark designed to
evaluate large language models on a broad spectrum of code-related
capabilities. It continuously collects problems from competitive
programming platforms—LeetCode, AtCoder, and CodeForces—using only
contests published *after* the training cutoffs of most evaluated
models, thereby eliminating data-leakage artifacts that plague static
coding benchmarks such as HumanEval and MBPP. Each problem falls into
one of four task categories: code generation, self-repair, code
execution, and test-output prediction. LiveCodeBench is used in our work
to evaluate whether the reasoning efficiency acquired through ExpThink
generalizes to complex, out-of-distribution programming tasks.

#### GPQA \[[38](#bib.bib36)\].

GPQA (Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A) is a rigorous multiple-choice
benchmark comprising 448 questions across biology, physics, and
chemistry, authored by domain specialists with doctoral-level expertise.
The questions are deliberately crafted to resist web-search assistance:
skilled non-experts who spent over 30 minutes searching the internet
achieved only 34% accuracy, while in-domain PhD experts reached
approximately 65%, underscoring the benchmark’s exceptional difficulty.
GPQA is used in our work to probe whether ExpThink improves deep
scientific reasoning in settings that demand genuine domain knowledge
rather than surface-level pattern matching.

## Appendix D Detailed Evaluation Protocol

#### Accuracy (Acc).

For each benchmark dataset, we measure accuracy as the proportion of
correctly answered problems:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{Acc}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}(\hat{y}_{i}=y_{i}),
``` |  | (5) |

where $`N`$ is the total number of problems, $`\hat{y}_{i}`$ is the
model’s predicted answer, $`y_{i}`$ is the ground-truth answer, and
$`\mathbf{1}(\cdot)`$ is the indicator function.

#### Average Token Length (Token).

We report the average number of tokens generated by the model across all
problems in a dataset:

|     |                                              |     |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \text{Token}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}l_{i},
       ```                                           |     | (6) |

where $`l_{i}`$ is the number of tokens in the model’s response for the
$`i`$-th problem.

#### Intelligence per Token (IPT).

To jointly evaluate accuracy and computational cost, we define
Intelligence per Token (IPT) as:

|     |                                                  |     |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \text{IPT}=\frac{\text{Acc}}{\text{Token}/1000},
       ```                                               |     | (7) |

where Acc denotes the Pass@1 accuracy (%) and Token denotes the average
output token length. Intuitively, IPT quantifies the accuracy gained per
1K tokens of generation, providing a unified measure of intelligence
density. A higher IPT indicates that the model achieves stronger
reasoning performance with fewer tokens, reflecting a more favorable
accuracy–efficiency trade-off. In the main results
(Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression")),
we report the IPT value averaged across all benchmark datasets for each
method.

#### Average Change Rate ($`\Delta`$).

To quantify the variation in performance introduced by a method relative
to the original base model, we define the change rate of a metric $`M`$
on a single dataset as:

|     |                                                              |     |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \text{CR}(M)=\frac{M_{\text{Method}}}{M_{\text{Vanilla}}}-1,
       ```                                                           |     | (8) |

where $`M\in\{\text{Acc},\text{Token}\}`$. The Average Change Rate
aggregates the change rates across all $`K=5`$ evaluation datasets:

|     |                                                      |     |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \Delta(M)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^{K}\text{CR}_{j}(M).
       ```                                                   |     | (9) |

#### Inference setup.

During inference, the maximum context size is limited to 16,384 tokens,
and the sampling temperature is fixed at 0.6. For the AIME dataset, due
to its relatively small sample size, we repeat the evaluation 16 times
and report the averaged results to reduce variance and improve
statistical reliability. Similarly, for the AMC dataset, we repeat the
evaluation 8 times and report the averaged results.

## Appendix E Detailed Descriptions of Baselines

All baseline methods are grounded in reinforcement learning (RL) and
address the problem of efficient reasoning from distinct perspectives.

#### LC-R1 \[[5](#bib.bib15)\].

LC-R1 (Length-Compressed R1) addresses reasoning efficiency by
augmenting the GRPO objective with two complementary reward signals. The
first is an explicit *length reward* that penalizes the total token
count of generated reasoning sequences, applying a global conciseness
pressure. The second is a *compression reward* that specifically targets
the elimination of redundant self-verification patterns—i.e., segments
where the model unnecessarily rechecks already-established
conclusions—without broadly suppressing productive reasoning steps. This
targeted decomposition allows LC-R1 to achieve approximately 50%
reduction in sequence length with only around 2% accuracy degradation.
We use the publicly released checkpoints LCR1-1.5B and LCR1-7B.

#### Laser \[[28](#bib.bib14)\].

Laser (Length-bAsed StEp rEward shaping) provides a unified framework
for efficient reasoning through step-level length-based reward shaping,
using a step function controlled by a target length as the primary
reward signal. Its extended variant, LASER-D, incorporates two
additional mechanisms: *dynamic adaptation*, where the reward
specification evolves continuously as model behavior changes throughout
training; and *difficulty-awareness*, which imposes heavier length
penalties on easier queries to encourage fast responses for simple
problems while preserving extended chain-of-thought for genuinely hard
ones. This explicit difficulty-conditioned reward design allows the
model to learn a problem-adaptive reasoning budget. We use the
checkpoints Laser-DE-L4096-1.5B and Laser-DE-L4096-7B, both trained on
the same dataset as ours.

#### AutoThink \[[41](#bib.bib18)\].

AutoThink is motivated by the observation that inserting a simple
ellipsis token into prompts can stochastically trigger either thinking
or no-thinking mode in R1-style models, revealing a latent
controllability in reasoning behavior. Building on this finding,
AutoThink proposes a three-stage reinforcement learning curriculum with
progressive reward shaping. Stage 1 employs batch-level reward balancing
to maintain the coexistence of both thinking and no-thinking modes
during early training; Stage 2 reinforces task accuracy within each mode
independently; Stage 3 introduces a length-aware reward to suppress
unnecessary computation and encourage direct responses for simpler
queries. Trained on the same dataset as ours, we use the checkpoints
Distill-R1-1.5B-AutoThink-Stage3 and Distill-R1-7B-AutoThink-Stage3.

#### AdaptThink \[[50](#bib.bib19)\].

AdaptThink is grounded in the empirical finding that forcing reasoning
models to always engage in extended chain-of-thought is suboptimal: for
simpler problems, skipping CoT entirely (*NoThinking* mode) can improve
both speed and accuracy. AdaptThink leverages RL with two complementary
components to exploit this observation: a *constrained optimization*
objective that nudges the model toward NoThinking responses while
preserving overall accuracy, and an *importance-sampling* scheme that
balances the ratio of Thinking versus NoThinking training samples to
enable stable exploration of both modes. Together, these enable the
model to adaptively select whether to invoke full chain-of-thought
reasoning or to respond directly, based on perceived problem difficulty.
Trained on the same dataset as ours, we use the checkpoints
AdaptThink-1.5B-delta0.05 and AdaptThink-7B-delta0.05.

#### JET \[[12](#bib.bib20)\].

JET (Just-Enough Thinking) is motivated by Evidence Accumulation Models
from cognitive science, which suggest that sufficient evidence for a
decision is often accumulated early in a reasoning sequence, rendering
subsequent steps redundant. JET operationalizes this insight through two
mechanisms: *trajectory truncation during rollout*, which exposes the
model to shorter, distributionally consistent reasoning paths during RL
training to overcome the distributional barrier that prevents naive
length rewards from generating compact rollouts; and a
*quality-controlled length reward*, which incentivizes conciseness while
explicitly preserving answer correctness. Rather than penalizing long
outputs after generation, JET shapes the model’s internal stopping
criterion so that it proactively terminates reasoning at the appropriate
point. We use the checkpoints JET-1.5B and JET-7B. JET has been accepted
at ICLR 2026.

## Appendix F Supplementary Experiments

### F.1 Difficulty-Aware Accuracy Analysis

| Method | Q1 (Easy) | Q2 | Q3 | Q4 | Q5 (Hard) | Overall |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Vanilla | 0.940 | 0.930 | 0.960 | 0.870 | 0.410 | 0.822 |
| ExpThink | 0.940 | 0.960 | 0.930 | 0.800 | 0.520 | 0.830 |
| Token $`\Delta`$ | $`-`$60.0% | $`-`$66.9% | $`-`$61.9% | $`-`$67.3% | $`-`$73.3% | $`-`$66.6% |

Table 4: Accuracy comparison between Vanilla and ExpThink across
difficulty levels on MATH-500 (1.5B model). Difficulty quintiles are
defined by Vanilla response length, where Q1 (shortest) represents easy
problems and Q5 (longest) represents the hardest problems that push the
Vanilla model toward its context limit.

The results reveal a key pattern in ExpThink’s difficulty-adaptive
behavior. On easy problems (Q1–Q3), both models achieve similar
accuracy, but ExpThink uses 60–67% fewer tokens, demonstrating efficient
compression without quality loss. On the hardest problems (Q5), ExpThink
achieves substantially higher accuracy (52.0% vs. 41.0%, a relative gain
of $`+`$26.8%) while simultaneously using 73.3% fewer tokens. This is
precisely the behavior intended by the difficulty-adaptive gradient
reweighting: easy problems receive suppressed gradients
(compression-first), while hard problems receive amplified gradients
(accuracy-first). The token reduction is actually largest on the hardest
quintile, because many Vanilla responses on hard problems hit the
16,384-token context limit and still fail—ExpThink finds shorter, more
direct solution paths that avoid the error-inducing overthinking
characteristic of the Vanilla model.

### F.2 Ablation Study Training Curves

Figure [8](#A6.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ F.2 Ablation Study Training Curves ‣ Appendix F Supplementary Experiments ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression")
presents the full training trajectories for all four $`r_{\text{pen}}`$
ablation settings ($`r_{\text{pen}}\in\{0.0,\,0.3,\,0.5,\,0.7\}`$ at
fixed $`\alpha=0.1`$) together with a standard GRPO advantage baseline
($`r_{\text{pen}}=0.5`$, standard group-normalised advantage), across
six metrics: validation AMC23 pass@1, policy entropy, mean critic score,
mean advantage, mean response length, and wall-clock time per step.

The most striking contrast is visible in the response length column.
Under $`r_{\text{pen}}=0.0`$, the response length collapses from roughly
7,600 tokens at step 1 to below 500 tokens by step 100, while AMC23
pass@1 simultaneously plummets from $`\sim`$55% to below 35%. This
confirms that assigning zero reward to incorrect responses removes the
incentive for the model to reason at all: once the policy discovers that
short, incorrect outputs cost nothing, it collapses into near-trivial
generations. In contrast, $`r_{\text{pen}}=0.5`$ (our full ExpThink
setting) shows a smooth, controlled compression: response length
decreases from $`\sim`$7,300 to $`\sim`$2,600 tokens over 364 steps
while AMC23 pass@1 improves steadily to above 65%. The
$`r_{\text{pen}}=0.3`$ setting occupies an intermediate regime—length
reduces to $`\sim`$2,000–3,000 tokens but accuracy stabilises around 55%
and remains consistently lower than the $`r_{\text{pen}}=0.5`$ setting,
indicating that insufficient penalty still impairs the incentive
structure. The $`r_{\text{pen}}=0.7`$ trajectory (steps 230–322) shows
the highest accuracy among all $`r_{\text{pen}}`$ settings but the least
length reduction, suggesting that an overly generous penalty weakens the
compression pressure.

The policy entropy column corroborates these observations:
$`r_{\text{pen}}=0.0`$ exhibits a rapid entropy collapse consistent with
mode collapse, while $`r_{\text{pen}}\in\{0.3,0.5,0.7\}`$ maintain
healthy entropy levels throughout training. The advantage column mirrors
the reward structure: under $`r_{\text{pen}}=0.0`$ advantages quickly
approach zero (the policy finds a trivial fixed point), whereas
$`r_{\text{pen}}=0.5`$ shows consistently non-trivial advantage signals
throughout.

The standard GRPO advantage row (purple, bottom) uses identical
hyperparameters to $`r_{\text{pen}}=0.5`$ but replaces the ExpThink
advantage with standard GRPO group-normalised advantage. Despite
reaching comparable AMC23 accuracy ($`\sim`$63%), its response length
converges to $`\sim`$4,600 tokens—nearly double that of ExpThink
($`\sim`$2,600 tokens)—demonstrating that the ExpThink advantage
formulation, rather than the discounted reward alone, is the key driver
of efficient compression.

Figure 8: Training curves for ablation experiments on
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B. Rows (top to bottom): four settings of
the discounted reward $`r_{\text{pen}}\in\{0.0,\,0.3,\,0.5,\,0.7\}`$
(red, orange, green, blue), followed by a standard GRPO advantage
baseline with $`r_{\text{pen}}=0.5`$ (purple). Columns (left to right):
(1) validation AMC23 pass@1 (sampled every 10 steps); (2) policy
entropy; (3) mean critic score; (4) mean advantage; (5) mean response
length (tokens); (6) wall-clock time per step (seconds). For dense
per-step metrics (columns 2–6), thin lines show raw values and thick
lines show smoothed trends. The $`r_{\text{pen}}=0.5`$ row (green,
highlighted) is the full ExpThink configuration and achieves the best
accuracy–efficiency trade-off. Note that $`r_{\text{pen}}=0.3`$ starts
from step 100 and $`r_{\text{pen}}=0.7`$ from step 230, as both runs
were resumed from earlier checkpoints.

### F.3 Experience Buffer Analysis

Figure 9: Response length dynamics of ExpThink on
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B.

We analyze the evolution of the training dynamics over 300 update steps
using the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B backbone, tracking the mean
response length at each step.

Figure [9](#A6.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ F.3 Experience Buffer Analysis ‣ Appendix F Supplementary Experiments ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression")
visualises the full training trajectory. The mean response length drops
from approximately 6.6k tokens at step 1 to around 1.8k tokens by
step 300—a reduction of roughly 73%—confirming that the
experience-guided reward progressively tightens the length budget as the
model accumulates shorter correct solutions. The mean length of
*correct* responses (dashed green) tracks consistently below the overall
mean; the shaded region between the two curves represents the
*compression gap*, i.e. the extra tokens spent by incorrect responses.
Both curves converge toward 1.5–2k tokens in the later training phase,
and the gap narrows substantially after step 150, indicating that the
model learns to be concise regardless of whether its answer is
ultimately correct.

As illustrated in Figure 3 of the main paper, the experience buffer
creates an implicit self-evolving curriculum. The running minimum
correct-solution length $`\ell_{q}^{*}`$ for each training problem
decreases monotonically over training steps, while the average
correct-solution length $`\bar{\ell}_{q}`$ at each step remains
substantially higher—this “compression gap” confirms that the model is
capable of shorter solutions but only intermittently achieves them
without the buffer’s guidance. Easy problems (as measured by pass rate)
tend to reach their minimum $`\ell_{q}^{*}`$ earlier in training,
causing the reward threshold for those problems to tighten quickly; hard
problems maintain a higher $`\ell_{q}^{*}`$ for longer, preserving a
generous budget that allows the model to focus on correctness rather
than brevity. This asymmetric tightening schedule emerges naturally from
the model’s own training trajectory, without any manual curriculum
design.

## Appendix G Case Studies

We present qualitative comparisons between the Vanilla baseline and
ExpThink across eight representative problems spanning all evaluated
benchmarks: five in-domain mathematical reasoning problems and three
out-of-distribution tasks. For each case, we display the full problem
statement, followed by the reasoning traces from both models. Long
traces are abbreviated with \[…\](omit $`N`$ tokens) where $`N`$ is the
estimated number of omitted tokens. Token counts are shown next to each
model label. Among the eight cases, three demonstrate scenarios where
both models answer correctly (Both Correct), illustrating that
ExpThink achieves equal accuracy at a fraction of the token cost; the
remaining five demonstrate scenarios where only ExpThink answers
correctly (ExpThink Correct, Vanilla Incorrect), showing that concise
reasoning also improves accuracy by eliminating error-inducing
overthinking.

Figure 10: Token usage comparison between Vanilla and ExpThink (1.5B) on
the eight selected case study examples. Red annotations show the
relative token reduction. Stars ($`\bigstar`$) indicate both-correct
cases; triangles ($`\blacktriangle`$) indicate ExpThink-only-correct
cases. The dashed line marks the 16,384-token context limit.

### G.1 In-Domain Mathematical Reasoning Cases

We select one problem from each of the five in-domain math benchmarks.
Two cases (AIME24 and AMC23) show that when both models answer
correctly, ExpThink uses dramatically fewer tokens—up to 92%
fewer—demonstrating efficient compression without quality loss. Three
cases (MATH-500, Minerva, OlympiadBench) show that ExpThink answers
correctly while Vanilla fails, illustrating how the experience-guided
curriculum eliminates the harmful overthinking loops that derail the
Vanilla model.

Figure 13: Case Study 3 (MATH-500, ExpThink Correct / Vanilla
Incorrect): ExpThink applies twin-prime reasoning in 829 tokens; Vanilla
uses 12,523 tokens and returns the wrong answer.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 14: Case Study 4 (Minerva Math, ExpThink Correct / Vanilla
Incorrect): ExpThink applies the magnitude formula in 892 tokens;
Vanilla uses 13,942 tokens and returns an answer wrong by $`10^{3}`$.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 15: Case Study 5 (OlympiadBench, ExpThink Correct / Vanilla
Incorrect): ExpThink correctly solves the hexagon problem in 1,525
tokens; Vanilla uses 15,361 tokens and returns the wrong answer.

### G.2 Out-of-Distribution Generalization Cases

We select one problem from each of the three OOD benchmarks. These tasks
were never seen during training, yet ExpThink generalizes its efficient
reasoning style to code generation (LiveCodeBench), graduate-level
science (GPQA-Diamond), and multi-domain knowledge (MMLU). Notably, on
MMLU, ExpThink achieves a 95% token reduction while maintaining
correctness, and on GPQA-Diamond, ExpThink succeeds where the verbose
Vanilla trace leads to an incorrect conclusion.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 16: Case Study 6 (MMLU, Both Correct): ExpThink answers in 768
tokens vs. Vanilla’s 15,493 tokens ($`-95.0\%`$).

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 17: Case Study 7 (GPQA-Diamond, ExpThink Correct / Vanilla
Incorrect): ExpThink finds the correct answer in 1,143 tokens; Vanilla
uses 13,024 tokens and returns the wrong answer.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 18: Case Study 8 (LiveCodeBench, Both Correct): ExpThink produces
correct code in 1,776 tokens vs. Vanilla’s 6,908 tokens ($`-74.3\%`$).

## NeurIPS Paper Checklist

1.  1.
    Claims
2.
    Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction
    accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?
3.
    Answer: \[Yes\]
4.
    Justification: The abstract and introduction clearly state the three
    core contributions: (1) identification of a structural limitation in
    existing RL-based CoT compression methods regarding discarded
    historical trajectory information; (2) the proposed ExpThink
    framework comprising a self-evolving compression curriculum, an
    experience-guided three-tier reward, and difficulty-adaptive
    advantage estimation; and (3) the experimental scope (mathematical
    reasoning benchmarks with three backbone models) and key
    quantitative claims (up to 77% response length reduction with
    consistent accuracy improvement, stable training dynamics, and up to
    $`3\times`$ higher IPT than the vanilla baseline). All claims are
    substantiated by
    Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression"),
    Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Discounted reward 𝑟_"pen". ‣ 4.3 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression")
    and
    Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.6 Generalization to out-of-distribution benchmarks. ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression")
    in
    Section [4](#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ ExpThink: Experience-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Compression").
5.
    Guidelines:

    - •
      The answer \[N/A\] means that the abstract and introduction do not
      include the claims made in the paper.
    - •
      The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims
      made, including the contributions made in the paper and important
      assumptions and limitations. A \[No\] or \[N/A\] answer to this
      question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.
    - •
      The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results,
      and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to
      other settings.
    - •
      It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as
      it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.
6.  2.
    Limitations
7.
    Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work
    performed by the authors?
8.
    Answer: \[Yes\]
9.
    Justification: Section 5 (Conclusion) contains a dedicated
    limitations paragraph discussing the following limitations: (1)
    training and evaluation are restricted to mathematical reasoning
    with verifiable answers, and transfer to interactive tool use or
    multimodal settings remains unconfirmed; (2) reliance on reliable
    answer verification, which may not hold for tasks with ambiguous or
    partially correct outputs; (3) the absence of a controlled
    comparison against DAPO under matched compute, which is left to
    future work; and (4) the tolerance margin $`\alpha`$ and discounted
    reward $`r_{\text{pen}}`$ are empirical choices, and a systematic
    study of $`\alpha`$ sensitivity across diverse domains is left to
    future work.

    Guidelines:

    - •
      The answer \[N/A\] means that the paper has no limitation while
      the answer \[No\] means that the paper has limitations, but those
      are not discussed in the paper.
    - •
      The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations”
      section in their paper.
    - •
      The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust
      the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g.,
      independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model
      well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding
      locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions
      might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.
    - •
      The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g.,
      if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few
      runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit
      assumptions, which should be articulated.
    - •
      The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the
      performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition
      algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or
      images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might
      not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online
      lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.
    - •
      The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the
      proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.
    - •
      If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of
      their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.
    - •
      While the authors might fear that complete honesty about
      limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a

      best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of
      transparency play an important role in developing norms that
      preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be
      specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning
      limitations.

31. 7.
    Experiment statistical significance
32.
    Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly
    defined or other appropriate information about the statistical
    significance of the experiments?
33.
    Answer: \[Yes\]
34.
    Justification: For evaluation, we address statistical variance
    differently based on dataset size. For small-scale benchmarks (AIME
    2024 and AMC 2023), we repeat evaluation 16 and 8 times respectively
    and report the mean to reduce random error caused by sampling
    variability. For larger benchmarks (e.g., MATH-500), the dataset
    size is sufficient to yield stable estimates, making repeated
    evaluation unnecessary. For training, we do not report error bars
    over multiple independent RL training runs due to the prohibitive
    computational cost (each run requires 8$`\times`$A800 GPUs for
    substantial wall-clock time), which is consistent with standard
    practice in the LLM RL literature.
35.
    Guidelines:

    - •
      The answer \[N/A\] means that the paper does not include
      experiments.
    - •
      The authors should answer \[Yes\] if the results are accompanied
      by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance
      tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims
      of the paper.
    - •
      The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing
      should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split,
      initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run
      with given experimental conditions).
    - •
      The method for calculating the error bars should be explained
      (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.)
    - •
      The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed
      errors).
    - •
      It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation
      or the standard error of the mean.
    - •
      It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it.
      The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than
      state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of
      errors is not verified.
    - •
      For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to
      show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield
      results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates).
    - •
      If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should
      explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the
      corresponding figures or tables in the text.

    Guidelines:

    - •

      address societal impact.
    - •
      Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious
      or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake
      profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment

      specific groups), privacy considerations, and security

      research and not tied to particular applications, let alone
      deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative

      legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of
      generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for
      disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out
      that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could
      enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.

      correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being
      used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following
      from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.

      discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of
      models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for
````
